steps.body: Counting is a pairing game: touch one toy, say one number. Every toy gets a number, and no toy gets two.
steps.narration: Counting is a pairing game: touch one toy, say one number. Every toy gets a number, and no toy gets two.

widget.prompt: Four toys to count. Place ONE counter for each toy.

commonCounts.feedback: One toy still has no counter — a toy without a counter is a toy without a number.
That is one counter too many; some toy has been counted twice.

widget.missFeedback: Place one counter at a time, saying the next number as you do.
widget.successFeedback: Four counters, four toys — every toy has exactly one number.

predict.prompt: If a toy is skipped while counting 4 toys, what happens?

options.label: The count comes out too small

predict.reveal: A skipped toy gets no number, so the last number said falls short of the true amount.

cml.actionGoal: Pair each object with exactly one number and trust the last number said for kch one to one.
invariants: A count pairs objects with number words one to one, and its last word names the whole group — which is why order, spacing, and arrangement can change without changing the answer for kch one to one.
misconceptions: Skipping or double-counting an object, recounting when nothing changed, or believing a spread-out group holds more.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one more object joined the group, what would the last counting word become?

widget.prompt: Why do we touch each toy while counting?

options.label: So every toy gets exactly one number
options.feedback: Correct — touching pairs each toy with one number, so nothing is skipped and nothing is counted twice.

options.label: To make the counting louder
options.feedback: Volume does not change the count; the touch is what keeps numbers and toys paired.

options.label: Because toys like being touched
options.feedback: The touch is for the counter, not the toy — it marks which toys already have a number.

options.label: To move the toys into a line
options.feedback: Counting works in any arrangement; the touch pairs, it does not tidy.

widget.prompt: Which record proves that every one of four toys was counted exactly once?

hotspots.label: 3 marks
hotspots.feedback: Three marks leave one toy without a count.

hotspots.label: 4 marks
hotspots.feedback: Four toys and four marks show one-to-one counting.

hotspots.label: 5 marks
hotspots.feedback: Five marks mean one of four toys was counted twice.

widget.missFeedback: Look for the choice that follows the counting rule exactly.
widget.successFeedback: Four toys and four marks show one-to-one counting.

widget.prompt: Mina counts her blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. How many blocks does she have?

options.feedback: Correct — the last number said, 9, tells how many blocks there are in all.
The count stops at 9; saying one more number would count a block that is not there.
That stops one number early — every block gets exactly one number, ending at 9.
That runs two past the count; the last number spoken is the answer, and it was 9.

widget.prompt: Start at 5. Hop forward 4 times by 1. Where do you land?

commonLandings.feedback: 8 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 9.
10 goes one complete hop too far. Count just 4 hops from 5 to land on 9.

widget.missFeedback: Start at 5 and count on 4: you land on 9.
widget.successFeedback: 5 and 4 more is 9 — each hop says the next counting number.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — count all 4 hops, one number per hop, to reach 9.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the count stops after exactly 4 hops, on 9.
